turns.user:
I'm a Product Manager (IC6) at Meta in the Bay Area. Google reached out to me. I wasn't looking and I'm happy where I am, but after interviewing they've made me an offer for a Senior Product Manager role (L6) in San Francisco.

At Meta I make $240,000 base, a bonus of about $36,000, and about $250,000/yr in vesting RSUs, so roughly $526,000/yr. About $200,000 of RSUs would vest in my next 12 months if I stayed.

The offer:
- Base salary: $235,000
- Target annual bonus: 20% of base ($47,000)
- New-hire RSUs: $1,080,000, vesting over 4 years
- No sign-on bonus

The job posting listed a base salary range of $183,000 to $271,000.

What the recruiter told me:
- Google gives annual equity refresh grants that stack over time, since each one vests over several years. The recruiter was clear that refreshes aren't guaranteed.

Compensation matters a lot to me. Is this a good offer? Should I accept it, negotiate, or walk away? If I negotiate, what exactly should I ask for, and how much?
turns.reply:
## Bottom line

**Negotiate. Don’t accept the first offer, but don’t walk away yet.**

This is a **good absolute offer**, but it is not an especially compelling *poaching offer* for someone who:

- is happy at Meta,
- wasn’t job-searching,
- already earns about $526,000,
- and would assume execution, culture, team, and refresh-grant risk by moving.

Google’s offer is about **$552,000 annualized** before future refreshes:

| Component | Annualized |
|---|---:|
| Base | $235,000 |
| Target bonus | $47,000 |
| Initial equity | $270,000 |
| **Total** | **$552,000** |

That is only **$26,000, or 5%, above your stated normal Meta compensation**. It is about **$76,000, or 16%, above your next-12-month Meta compensation of $476,000**, because only $200,000 of Meta stock will vest during that period.

For a happy, passive candidate, **5% ongoing upside is not enough compensation for switching risk**, in my judgment.

Market data is imperfect, but it points in the same direction: Levels.fyi currently reports approximately **$606,000 median Bay Area compensation for Google L6 PMs**. A separate recent US dataset puts L6 PM median compensation around $514,000 and the 90th percentile around $671,000. So this is respectable, but not an obvious top-of-band L6 offer. ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/san-francisco-bay-area?utm_source=openai))

## First: confirm the actual equity schedule

Before evaluating or countering, get these details in writing:

1. **What percentage of the $1.08 million vests in each of years 1–4?**
2. What is the first vest date?
3. Is the grant converted to shares using a price before or after your start date?
4. When would you first become eligible for a refresh grant?
5. Is your first annual bonus prorated?
6. Does the sign-on or equity have any special repayment/clawback terms?

Do not assume “over four years” means 25% each year.

For illustration:

### If it vests evenly

Your target compensation is:

- Year 1: $552,000
- Year 2: $552,000
- Year 3: $552,000
- Year 4: $552,000

### If it is front-loaded 38% / 32% / 20% / 10%

Your compensation before refreshes would be:

| Year | Equity | Base + target bonus | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | $410,400 | $282,000 | **$692,400** |
| 2 | $345,600 | $282,000 | **$627,600** |
| 3 | $216,000 | $282,000 | **$498,000** |
| 4 | $108,000 | $282,000 | **$390,000** |

That would make the first two years attractive, but create a serious year-three/year-four cliff. Refreshes may help, but Google’s own description of its compensation process indicates equity refreshes involve modeled recommendations, manager discretion, and review—not an entitlement. Treat refreshes as upside, not as part of your guaranteed offer valuation. ([services.google.com](https://services.google.com/fh/files/blogs/pay_equity_info_sheet.pdf?utm_source=openai))

## How strong are the individual components?

### Base: somewhat weak

Your $235,000 offer is:

- $5,000 below your Meta base;
- about 59% of the way through the posted $183,000–$271,000 range;
- not particularly aggressive for an experienced Bay Area L6 hire.

Current comparable Google Senior PM listings advertise roughly $192,000–$278,000 base plus a 20% bonus and equity, although individual postings differ. ([google.com](https://www.google.com/about/careers/applications/jobs/results/112598809917170374-senior-product-manager-generative-ai-google-cloud?company=Google&company=Google+Fiber&company=YouTube%C2%B0ree%3DBACHELORS&distance=50&employment_type=FULL_TIME&gclsrc=aw.ds&hl=en_US&jlo=en_US&location=United+States&page=1&q=&sort_by=date&src=Online%2FHouse+Ads%2FBKWS&utm_source=openai))

I would expect you to push toward **$250,000–$260,000**.

### Bonus: probably standardized

The 20% target is normal for the role and likely not negotiable. Focus elsewhere.

### Equity: good, but not enough to make the overall package exceptional

The $1.08 million grant sounds large, but annualized it is $270,000.

To merely match your normal $526,000 compensation:

- Cash compensation at Google: $282,000
- Required annual equity: $244,000
- Required four-year grant: **$976,000**

So the offer exceeds your current run-rate by only **$104,000 over four years**, before considering a sign-on.

For a **15% premium** over your Meta run-rate, Google would need to provide roughly $605,000 annually. At the offered base, that requires a four-year equity grant of approximately **$1.29 million**.

That is a useful, defensible negotiation target.

### Sign-on: clear omission

The lack of a sign-on is the most obvious gap, especially because:

- you are giving up about $200,000 of Meta equity vesting over the next 12 months;
- you may forfeit some bonus depending on departure timing;
- Google’s grant may not begin vesting immediately;
- you were not actively looking and therefore need a real inducement to move.

Google may respond that its first-year equity replaces your Meta vesting. That is partly fair, but a cash sign-on still addresses timing and switching risk.

## What I would ask for

### Opening counter

Ask for:

- **Base: $260,000**
- **New-hire equity: $1.4 million**
- **Sign-on bonus: $100,000–$150,000**
- Bonus remains 20%

At $260,000 base and $1.4 million in stock, the recurring annualized package would be:

- Base: $260,000
- Bonus: $52,000
- Equity: $350,000
- **Annualized total: $662,000**
- Plus sign-on

That is an aggressive but credible opening position: it remains near the reported upper portion—not outside the universe—of L6 PM compensation.

### Reasonable settlement

I would regard something around the following as a good negotiated outcome:

- **Base: $250,000–$255,000**
- **Equity: $1.25 million–$1.35 million**
- **Sign-on: $75,000–$100,000**

For example:

| Component | Amount |
|---|---:|
| Base | $250,000 |
| Bonus | $50,000 |
| Annualized equity on $1.3M grant | $325,000 |
| **Recurring annualized TC** | **$625,000** |
| Sign-on | **$75,000–$100,000** |

That creates a meaningful premium over staying at Meta and better compensates you for the risk of moving.

### If Google says base is constrained

Prioritize in this order:

1. **More initial equity**
2. **Cash sign-on**
3. Base salary

Every additional $100,000 of equity adds $25,000 to four-year annualized compensation. A $100,000 sign-on gives you certainty immediately, whereas refresh equity is discretionary.

A fallback structure could be:

- $245,000–$250,000 base
- $1.3 million equity
- $100,000 sign-on

## Suggested wording

You can say:

> I’m genuinely excited about the role and team. At the same time, I wasn’t actively looking, I’m happy at Meta, and my current compensation is approximately $526,000 annually, with about $200,000 of Meta equity vesting over the next 12 months.
>
> As structured, the Google package is approximately $552,000 annualized before refreshes, so the ongoing premium is relatively modest given the risk and forfeited compensation involved in making a move. The lack of a sign-on also makes the transition harder.
>
> To make the move compelling, I’d like to see whether we can get to $260,000 in base, $1.4 million in new-hire equity, and a $125,000 sign-on bonus. I understand there may be constraints between components, and I’m flexible about shifting value toward equity or sign-on if base is less flexible. If we can get close to that overall package, I would be prepared to move forward promptly.

Only include the last sentence if you genuinely would accept near those numbers.

## Additional leverage you should use

### Your upcoming Meta vest dates

Determine exactly when the next large Meta tranches vest. If, for example, $50,000–$100,000 vests within a few months, you have two options:

- negotiate a Google start date after that vest; or
- ask Google to replace the forfeited tranche through sign-on or additional equity.

A later start date can sometimes be worth more than winning another $10,000 of base.

### Your level and scope

Meta IC6 and Google L6 are not mechanically identical. If your Meta scope is already organization-wide, involves several teams, or resembles Google L7 scope, it is reasonable to ask:

> Can you help me understand how the committee mapped my current scope to L6, and whether L7 was considered?

Don’t make this your primary compensation counter unless the proposed Google role genuinely has L7-level scope. A level increase is much harder than a compensation increase, but it has much larger long-term consequences.

## When I would accept or decline

### Accept if

- The role is at least as attractive as your Meta role, **and**
- the vesting schedule is favorable, **and**
- Google gets the package to roughly **$600,000–$625,000 recurring annualized value**, or compensates for a slightly lower recurring number with a substantial sign-on.

### Consider accepting the current package only if

- it has heavily front-loaded vesting;
- you strongly prefer the team, product, manager, or career trajectory;
- you believe Google materially improves your promotion or future-option value;
- and you are comfortable with the later equity cliff.

### Stay at Meta if

Google makes little or no movement and the roles are otherwise comparable.

The current offer is not bad, but **it is not financially compelling enough by itself to justify leaving a job you like**. Your strongest posture is truthful: you are willing to stay. Negotiate firmly, value refresh grants at zero in your downside case, and require the written offer—not verbal projections—to make the economics work.

turns.user: Update: I told the recruiter I'd be walking away from about $200,000 of RSUs that would vest in the next 12 months. Final offer: base $240,000, RSUs raised to $1,280,000 (vesting over 4 years), and no sign-on bonus. They said this is their best offer. Should I take it?
turns.reply:
## My take

**This is now a genuinely good offer.** I would **take it if you are at least neutral-to-positive on the role, manager, team, and career trajectory**. I would stay at Meta only if you materially prefer the Meta job or have serious concerns about Google’s role or organization.

I would not keep pushing compensation after they have explicitly called this their best offer. You successfully improved it by a meaningful amount.

## The comparison

### Annualized over four years

| | Meta | Final Google offer |
|---|---:|---:|
| Base | $240,000 | $240,000 |
| Target/expected bonus | $36,000 | $48,000 |
| Annualized equity | $250,000 | $320,000 |
| **Annualized total** | **$526,000** | **$608,000** |

Google is approximately:

- **$82,000 per year higher**
- **15.6% above your current run rate**
- **$328,000 higher over four years**, assuming your Meta compensation remains around $526,000 and excluding refresh grants at either company

The original offer was only about 5% above Meta. The final offer is roughly 16% above. That crosses from “not enough to induce a happy employee to move” into “meaningful switching premium.”

It also lands almost exactly at the currently reported Bay Area median of approximately **$606,000 for Google L6 PMs**. So it is a strong, market-level L6 package, though not an extraordinary top-of-band one. ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/san-francisco-bay-area?utm_source=openai))

## The $200,000 you’re walking away from

Be careful not to double-count this.

The $200,000 in Meta stock is what you receive **if you stay**. It should be compared with the Google equity that vests during the same period—not added on top of your normal Meta compensation as a separate loss.

If Google’s stock vested evenly, your first 12 months would be:

- Base: $240,000
- Target bonus: $48,000
- Equity: $320,000
- **Total: $608,000**

Compared with staying at Meta for the next 12 months:

- Base: $240,000
- Bonus: approximately $36,000
- Equity vesting: approximately $200,000
- **Total: approximately $476,000**

That would put Google about **$132,000 ahead in year one**, despite forfeiting the Meta stock.

### If Google uses front-loaded vesting

Google new-hire grants are commonly reported as vesting approximately **38% / 32% / 20% / 10%**, although your actual written grant schedule controls. ([thesimplemoney.com](https://thesimplemoney.com/employers/google/gsu-grants-and-vesting-schedule?utm_source=openai))

Under that schedule:

| Year | Google equity | Base + target bonus | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | $486,400 | $288,000 | **$774,400** |
| 2 | $409,600 | $288,000 | **$697,600** |
| 3 | $256,000 | $288,000 | **$544,000** |
| 4 | $128,000 | $288,000 | **$416,000** |
| **Four-year average** | **$320,000** | **$288,000** | **$608,000** |

If that is your schedule, Google more than compensates for the forfeited Meta stock in the first year. The real issue becomes the **year-three/year-four decline**, not your initial forfeiture.

You should confirm the exact schedule in the offer documentation before signing.

## The decision rule I would use

### Take Google if:

- You consider the role and manager at least as good as the Meta alternatives.
- The scope is appropriate for L6 and gives you a credible path to larger scope or L7.
- You are comfortable with the vesting cliff.
- You are willing to remain long enough to collect most of the initial grant.
- There are no warning signs about the organization, mandate, or manager.

### Stay at Meta if:

- You materially prefer your current work, manager, or work-life balance.
- The Google role seems less stable or less strategically important.
- You believe your Meta compensation will soon increase substantially through refreshes or promotion.
- You are likely to leave Google after one or two years and therefore are evaluating this mainly as a short-term move.
- You would resent having moved if Google refreshes prove disappointing.

Because you are already happy, you do **not** need to move simply because the offer is financially better. But the financial case against moving has largely disappeared.

## How to handle refresh grants

Value them at **zero for purposes of deciding whether the guaranteed offer is acceptable**.

That is conservative, but appropriate because:

- The recruiter expressly said they are not guaranteed.
- The amount will depend on performance, company processes, level, and potentially stock appreciation.
- Refreshes may soften the later vesting cliff, but you cannot know by how much.

Google publicly describes equity refreshes as part of its annual compensation-planning process, but the modeled amount can be adjusted rather than functioning as a contractual entitlement. ([services.google.com](https://services.google.com/fh/files/blogs/pay_equity_info_sheet.pdf?utm_source=openai))

The good news is that the offer works reasonably well without assuming refreshes. Refreshes would be upside and potentially the mechanism that makes years three and four acceptable.

## One final thing to request

I would **not submit another monetary counter**. But because there is no sign-on, make one final logistical request:

> Since there isn’t flexibility for a sign-on bonus, I’d like to coordinate the start date to minimize forfeited compensation at Meta. My next vest is on [date]. Can we set my start date shortly after that?

If a significant Meta tranche vests relatively soon, this could be worth tens of thousands of dollars and may be easier for Google to approve than additional compensation.

Also confirm in writing:

1. Exact equity percentages by year  
2. First vest date and vesting frequency  
3. How the share count is calculated  
4. Whether your first bonus will be prorated  
5. The first cycle in which you can receive a refresh grant  
6. Any repayment or clawback provisions  

## Recommendation

**Financially, I would now lean yes.** The offer has gone from $552,000 to approximately **$608,000 annualized**, a $56,000-per-year improvement. It is about **16% above your Meta run rate**, while year-one compensation should comfortably replace the $200,000 Meta vest you would forgo.

My practical answer:

- **Role/team at least equally attractive:** Accept.
- **Role is somewhat worse but tolerable:** Probably stay—the 16% premium may not compensate for daily dissatisfaction.
- **Role creates stronger long-term scope or promotion opportunities:** Accept enthusiastically.
- **Major uncertainty about manager, mandate, or reorg exposure:** Stay at Meta.

This is no longer an offer I would walk away from merely because the compensation is inadequate. The remaining decision is primarily about **job quality and career value**, not whether Google has paid enough to make the move financially credible.
